articles: Before a consonant SOUND, for one unspecific countable thing.
a dog, a university, a one-way street
Before a vowel SOUND (it depends on sound, not spelling).
an apple, an hour, an MP
A specific or already-known thing, or something unique.
the moose we saw, the sun, the Rockies
Plurals and uncountables in general; most names of people, cities and countries; meals; languages.
Dogs bark. Water is wet. She speaks French. We had lunch.
confusables: affect / effect
'Affect' is usually a verb (to influence); 'effect' is usually a noun (a result).
The weather affected the game. The effect was dramatic.
its / it's
'Its' shows possession; 'it's' is 'it is' or 'it has'.
The dog wagged its tail. It's late.
their / there / they're
Their = belonging to them; there = place; they're = they are.
Their car is over there. They're leaving.
your / you're
Your = belonging to you; you're = you are.
Your coat is here. You're early.
then / than
'Then' is about time; 'than' compares.
First we ate, then we left. She is taller than me.
to / too / two
To = direction or part of a verb; too = also or excessively; two = the number 2.
I went to the store too. It was too late. Two of us stayed.
lose / loose
'Lose' is a verb (to misplace); 'loose' means not tight.
Don't lose the key. The screw is loose.
accept / except
'Accept' = receive or agree; 'except' = excluding.
I accept the offer. Everyone came except Sam.
principal / principle
'Principal' = head or main; 'principle' = a rule or belief.
The principal spoke. It's a matter of principle.
complement / compliment
'Complement' completes something; 'compliment' is praise.
Red wine complements steak. She paid me a compliment.
advice / advise
'Advice' is a noun; 'advise' is a verb.
I need advice. I advise you to wait.
who / whom
'Who' is the subject; 'whom' is the object (after a preposition or verb).
Who called? To whom did you speak?
fewer / less
'Fewer' for countable things; 'less' for uncountable.
fewer apples, less water
lie / lay
'Lie' (lie, lay, lain) = recline; 'lay' (lay, laid, laid) = put something down.
I lie down. I lay the book on the table.
farther / further
'Farther' is physical distance; 'further' is extent or degree (also distance in everyday use).
It's farther down the road. Let's discuss it further.
among / between
'Between' for two (or clear individual relationships); 'among' for a group.
between you and me, among the trees
degrees: Three or more syllables, most two-syllable words
good, better, best · bad, worse, worst · far, farther/further, farthest/furthest · little, less, least · many/much, more, most
modals: I can swim. Can I sit here?
past ability, polite request, weaker possibility
She could run fast. Could you help?
May I come in? It may rain.
Shall we go? Tenants shall pay rent monthly.
You should rest. She should be home by now.
Would you mind? I would go if I could.
You must wear a helmet. He must be tired.
plurals: Ends in s, x, z, ch, sh
bus → buses, box → boxes, church → churches
leaf → leaves, knife → knives (but roof → roofs, chief → chiefs)
potato → potatoes, hero → heroes; photo → photos, piano → pianos
man → men, woman → women, child → children, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice, person → people, sheep → sheep, deer → deer, fish → fish
cactus → cacti or cactuses, analysis → analyses, criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena
water, advice, information, furniture, news, luggage (use 'a piece of' to count)

pos.def: Names a person, place, thing, idea or quality.
pos.name: Noun
pos.note: Types: common, proper (Canada), countable (book) and uncountable (water), collective (flock), abstract (freedom).

pos.def: Takes the place of a noun so you don't have to repeat it.
pos.name: Pronoun
pos.note: Types: personal (I, you, they), possessive (mine, theirs), reflexive (myself), relative (who, which), demonstrative (this, that), interrogative (what, whom).

pos.def: Shows an action, an event or a state of being.
pos.name: Verb
pos.note: Main verbs carry the meaning; auxiliary (helping) verbs such as be, have and do build tenses; modal verbs (can, must) add possibility or obligation.

pos.def: Describes or limits a noun or pronoun.
pos.name: Adjective
pos.note: Can come before the noun or after a linking verb. Many have comparative and superlative forms (cold, colder, coldest).

pos.def: Describes a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence; often tells how, when, where or how much.
pos.name: Adverb
pos.note: Many end in -ly, but not all (fast, well, often, here).

pos.def: Links a noun or pronoun to another word and shows place, time, direction or relationship.
pos.name: Preposition
pos.note: A preposition is followed by an object: in the house, with her, by noon.

pos.name: Conjunction
pos.note: Coordinating: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Subordinating: because, although, when, if, while.

pos.def: A short exclamation that expresses emotion; it stands apart from the grammar of the sentence.
pos.name: Interjection
pos.note: Usually followed by an exclamation mark or a comma.

pos.def: Introduces a noun and shows which one, how many or whose. Articles (a, an, the) are the most common determiners.
pos.name: Determiner
pos.note: Some grammars fold determiners into adjectives. Modern grammar treats them as their own class.

punctuation: Ends a statement. Also used in many abbreviations (Dr., etc.).
Separates items in a list, joins clauses with a conjunction, sets off introductory phrases and extra information. Don't use a comma alone to join two full sentences.
Links two closely related full sentences, or separates items in a list that already contains commas.
Introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation after a full clause.
Shows possession (the dog's bone) and contractions (don't). Never makes a plain plural.
Joins words into a compound (well-known author) or splits a word at a line break.
Marks a break in thought or sets off extra information. (An en dash – shows ranges: 2020–2026.)
Mark spoken words or titles of short works. Canadian and American writing use double quotation marks first and single inside them; British usually reverses this.
Shows strong feeling or emphasis. Use sparingly.
spelling: Canadian follows British (but a measuring device is a meter everywhere).
Canadian follows American. Oxford British also accepts -ize.
Check is still used for other meanings.
Canadian uses program for all senses.
Canadian doubles the l, like British.

ex: She walks to work every day.
tenses.form: base verb (+ s/es for he, she, it)
tenses.name: Present Simple

ex: They are staying with friends this week.
tenses.name: Present Continuous
tenses.use: Actions happening right now, temporary situations, and firm future plans.

tenses.name: Present Perfect
tenses.use: Past events that matter now, life experience, and unfinished time periods.

ex: I have been waiting for an hour.
He has been running; he is out of breath.
tenses.name: Present Perfect Continuous
tenses.use: How long something has been going on, or an action that just stopped and left a visible result.

tenses.form: past form (verb + ed, or an irregular form)
tenses.name: Past Simple
tenses.use: Completed actions at a definite time in the past.

ex: I was cooking when the power went out.
tenses.name: Past Continuous
tenses.use: An action in progress in the past, often interrupted by another.

ex: She had left before I arrived.
tenses.name: Past Perfect
tenses.use: An action finished before another past action or time.

ex: He had been working for hours when the bell rang.
tenses.name: Past Perfect Continuous
tenses.use: How long something had been going on before a point in the past.

tenses.name: Future Simple
tenses.note: 'Be going to' + base verb is common for plans and for predictions based on evidence: 'Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.'
tenses.use: Predictions, promises and decisions made at the moment of speaking.

ex: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Vancouver.
tenses.name: Future Continuous
tenses.use: An action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future.

ex: By June, she will have graduated.
tenses.name: Future Perfect
tenses.use: An action that will be finished by a certain time in the future.

ex: By next month, I will have been living here for ten years.
tenses.name: Future Perfect Continuous
tenses.use: How long something will have been going on by a point in the future.
